title: the bridge
hook: five days, a whole army of builders, and the stories people added later

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, promised. The ocean said it couldn't change what it was, but gave your line, I'll hold it up, and named Nala as the builder.

Nala steps forward, and what he says is quietly funny. The ocean is right. I'm Vishvakarma's son, and I have my father's skill. I can build this. Then he adds, more or less: nobody asked me, so I didn't mention it. An army has been staring at an impossible sea, and the one person who could solve it was standing in the crowd, waiting to be asked. Then the work begins.
screen: `NALA STEPS FORWARD.` → `NOBODY ASKED ME.` → `THE WORK BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki loves the noise of it. The monkeys and bears pour into the forests and tear up trees by the thousand: palms, ashokas, flowering trees of every kind. They drag boulders down from the hills and heave them into the water with a sound like thunder. Some hold measuring lines while others lay the stones. And he counts the days. Fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. In five days it's done: a bridge a hundred yojanas long and ten wide, straight across the sea. The gods watch from the sky, amazed, and the army crosses to the shore of Lanka. Two things you may have heard aren't in Valmiki. One is the squirrel, who rolls in the sand and shakes it onto the bridge, and Rama strokes its back, and the stripes are his fingers. The other is the stones that float because Rama's name is written on them. Both come from later retellings and oral tradition, and devotees tell them as lessons in devotion: no gift is too small, and the name carries weight. It's worth knowing which is which. Today the line of shoals between Rameswaram in India and Mannar in Sri Lanka is called Rama Setu, Rama's bridge, in Hindu tradition. People hold different views about what that chain of shoals is, and those arguments go on. What Valmiki gives is simpler: a whole people, five days, one bridge.
screen: `TREES, BOULDERS AND THUNDER.` · `FIVE DAYS, A HUNDRED YOJANAS.` · `THE SQUIRREL CAME LATER.` · `RAMA SETU TODAY.` · then, large: `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ONE BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people around you, at work, at home, in your neighborhood: is there a Nala among them, someone with a skill nobody has thought to ask about? Picture their face kindly and let the question rest, what could I ask them, then come back to the breath, one stone at a time.
The bridge. Setu. Built in five days by an army of monkeys and bears under Nala, a hundred yojanas long, carried by the ocean that promised to hold it up.
Your line: a whole people, one bridge. Tomorrow, a step back in time, into Ravana's hall. That's day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Rameswaram and Dhanushkodi on India's southeastern coast, linked by tradition to the bridge, and the squirrel's story is a common children's tale.

chat.says: Who actually built the bridge to Lanka in the Ramayana, and how long did it take?
options: Nala led it, with the whole army of monkeys and bears, in five days.
Hanuman built it alone, carrying every stone across in one night.
Rama built it himself, and it took the army a whole year.
chat.meaning: Valmiki gives the whole people a part: monkeys and bears haul trees and boulders under Nala, and the bridge is done in five days.

Nala.meaning: Vishvakarma's son, the builder of the bridge

yojanas.meaning: an old Indian measure of distance, many miles each

Rameswaram.meaning: a coastal town in India linked by tradition to the bridge

Rama Setu.meaning: the shoals between India and Sri Lanka, called Rama's bridge

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 22 (Nala's offer; the building of the bridge in five days; the crossing)

notes: Nala's remark that he wasn't asked, so he didn't speak of his skill: paraphrased; confirm.
The daily counts (14, 20, 21, 22, 23 yojanas) and the bridge's size (100 by 10 yojanas): confirm against the vulgate.

The squirrel story and the floating stones inscribed with Rama's name are described as later retellings, not Valmiki; a Keeper may want to name specific sources (e.g. regional Ramayanas, oral tradition).
Rama Setu / Adam's Bridge: the script says only that many Hindus call the shoals Rama Setu and that views differ; it takes no position on their origin.
Rama's worship of Shiva at Rameswaram is left out; it is not in the vulgate's account of the building.
